units.la: Quum vana pro veris saepè valeant, maximè in bellis: vt dixit Liuius: Quàc[?] vt belli, sic auditionis famaeque quae mobilitate viget, viresque acquirit eundo, inania multa sint: non sine scitu voluntateque Superiorum, edita est haec Orationis, de Disputatione Heydelbergensi de Eucharistica controuersia, quasi quaedam synopsis: vt eadem opera, & satisfieret iis qui citra praeiudicium, rem totam, vt ea acta fuit, cognoscere & dijudicare, cupiunt: & haberent caeteri, qui fabularum quarundam, hoc semestri sparsarum, auditione non nihil obstupefacti sunt, cur earum Mercurijs, Ciceronianum illud regerant: Ementiuntur saepè homines, in eos, quos oderunt. Tu, quisquis es pie Lector, vnà nobiscum comprecare Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum, vt nobis quidem adiungere pergat veritatis comites, sapientiam & constantiam: ijs autem, qui seipsos & alios, fabellis inanibus lactant, det vt vel confusionis suae metu adducti, istud Augustini (veritate vincibonû est) tandem amplectantur & sequantur: nec eam pertinaciter oppugnando, dedecus & noxam certissimam sibi ipsis accersant, Vale optime.
units.tr: Since empty things often prevail over true ones, especially in wars (as Livy said), so too with rumour and reputation, which thrive on their fickleness and gain strength as they go, many of them are empty. This synopsis of the Oration delivered at the most famous Academy, on the Heidelberg Disputation concerning the Eucharistic controversy, has been published, not without the knowledge and approval of our superiors, as a kind of summary. The aim is twofold: to satisfy those who wish to learn and judge the whole matter, as it was actually conducted, without prejudice; and to give the rest, who have been not a little startled by the hearing of certain fables scattered abroad this half-year, a reason why these Mercuries (messengers) repeat that saying of Cicero: "Men often lie about those whom they hate." You, whoever you are, pious reader, pray along with us that Christ Jesus our Lord would continue to join us as companions of truth, wisdom and steadfastness; and for those who flatter themselves and others with empty fables, may he grant that, moved at least by fear of their own confusion, they finally embrace and follow that saying of Augustine, "Truth conquers all things" (veritate vincibonû est), and do not, by stubbornly assailing it, bring upon themselves disgrace and most certain harm. Farewell, best of readers.

units.la: ORATIONIS, QUA FINEM IMPOSUI DISPUTATIONIBUS DE CONTROVERSIA EUCHARISTICA, Anno 1584. April. 15. delineatio.
units.tr: Oration with which I brought the disputations on the Eucharistic controversy to a close, in the year 1584, 15 April: an outline.

units.la: ILLUSTRISSIME PRIN-ceps & clementissime Domine: Magnifice Domine Rector; Generose D. Baro: amplissimi & prudentissimi D. Consiliarij; Et clarissimi omnium ordinum Doctores & Professores in hac Heydelbergensi Academia: heroica Nobilitas, ingeniorum & virtutum stemmatumque laude florentissima: Hospites lectissimi & ob eximia decora suspiciendi; Tuque literata iuuentus, Ecclesiae & Reipub. Christianae seminarium magis magisque efflorescens. Si per omnem meam vitam, ullo alio tempore, diu, multum & optime praemeditata Oratione mihi utendum fuit: hoc enim verò tempore eiusmodi Oratione mihi opus esse intelligo: quo videlicet, summa manus & veluti Catastrophe, σὺν θεῷ[?], imponenda est publicae huic de controversia Eucharistica Disputationi; tum quia Illustriss. Principis heroica clemen-tia, & erga nos bonitate, nobis utendum est, & habenda occupationum ciuilium quoque & maximè necessariarum ratio quaedam: tum, quia praeter huius & aliarum Academiarum usitatum morem, saepè nu-merò iam est disputatum: tum quia illi, quorum causa potissimum Disputatio instituta fuit, eadem Argumenta sexcenties repetiuerunt: & nunc occu-pationibus Ecclesiasticis paschalibus, sese distrahi queruntur; tum denique, quoniam a nobis, octies iam, disputandi copia illis (quorum equidem fuerat differendi copiam nobis facere, & sua tueri dogmata) facta est, quum superioribus annis, nostris hominibus, supplicitèr sese audiri petentibus, ne quidē[?] Colloquij, quod horulę vnius spacio & vsura constaret, potestatè a suis prædecessoribus, & a se factam esse, probè meminerit pars altera: quæ quod hoc tempore, toties & tam humaniter, est ad disputandum admissa, inuitata, auditaque, id verò Illu-strissimi nostri Principis summæ benignitati, accep-tum ferre, gratóque animo agnoscere, debet.
units.tr: Most illustrious Prince and most gracious Lord; Magnificent Lord Rector; noble Lord Baron; most distinguished and prudent Lords Councillors; and most renowned Doctors and Professors of all faculties in this Heidelberg Academy; heroic nobility, flourishing in the praise of talents, virtues and ancestry; most select guests, to be admired for your outstanding graces; and you, learned youth, the nursery of the Church and the Christian commonwealth, growing more and more vigorous. If at any other time in my whole life I have had to use a speech long and carefully prepared, it is now that I understand I need such a speech: at this moment the final touch, and as it were the conclusion, is to be placed upon this public disputation on the Eucharistic controversy (God willing). This is so, first, because we must make use of the heroic clemency of the illustrious Prince and his goodness towards us, and take some account of civil and very necessary occupations as well; secondly, because, contrary to the customary practice of this and other academies, the disputation has often now been held; thirdly, because those for whose sake the disputation was chiefly instituted have repeated the same arguments six hundred times, and now complain that they are distracted by their Easter ecclesiastical duties; and lastly, because, eight times now, an opportunity for disputing has been given to them (who ought to have given us the opportunity of debating and defending their own doctrines). For in previous years, when our men begged to be heard, the other side well remembers that they and their predecessors had refused even a colloquy that would have taken up the space and use of a single hour. That they have now been admitted, invited and heard so often and so courteously to dispute ought to be acknowledged and gratefully credited to the great kindness of our illustrious Prince.

units.la: Verùm enimuero, quum res ipsa loquatur, me destitui hoc tempore, & ocio, ad meditandum: & libris, consiliarijs videlicet meis, ad eos consulen-dos: ita me Deus bene amet, nec ingenij, nec facun-diæ, sed dulcissimæ promissionis Domini nostri Iesu Christi (Dabitur vobis illa hora quod loquamini: non enim vos estis ij qui loquuntur: sed Spiritus Patris vestri, is est qui loquitur in vobis) fiducia adductus & confirmatus: dicam breuiter verèque, de istius disputationis, in qua sementem pię & verę doctrinę de S. Eucharistia, mihi videor fecisse, successu & fructu.
units.tr: But truly, since the matter itself speaks, I have had no leisure at this time to meditate, and no books, namely my counsellors, to consult. Yet, so may God love me, I was encouraged and strengthened not by talent or eloquence, but by the sweet promise of our Lord Jesus Christ (It will be given you in that hour what you should speak: for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you). I will say briefly and truly what I think I have achieved, in success and fruit, in this disputation, in which I seem to have sown the seed of the pure and true doctrine of the Holy Eucharist.

units.la: Erit autem omnium vestrum, quotquot haud dubiè in solius Iesu Christi nomine congregati adestis, eximiæ pietatis, prudentiæ & candoris, ea quæ nullius mortalium insectandi aut lædendi gratia, dicturus sum, in optimam partem, ita ut decet sanctos, accipere & interpretari. Vt enim vos omnes minimè fugit illud diuinum præceptum: τὸ ἐπιεικὲς ἡμῶν[?], Moderata æquitas vestra nota sit omnibus hominibus. Dominus propè est: Ita mei muneris est, quæcunque sunt vera, quæcunque veneranda, quæcunque amabilia & εὔφημα[?] sunt, tum profiteri tum præstare. Dominus Iesus Christus det, vt ipsi grata, hoc est, vera & πρὸς ἀλῆ[?] ad diuini nominis sanctificationem, edicere possim.
units.tr: All of you, whoever you are who are assembled here undoubtedly in the name of Jesus Christ alone, of outstanding piety, prudence and candour, will accept and interpret in good part what I am about to say, not for the sake of attacking or harming anyone, as befits saints. For, as none of you is unaware of that divine precept, "Let your moderation be known to all men; the Lord is at hand," it is my duty to profess and perform whatever is true, whatever is worthy of respect, whatever is lovely and of good report. May the Lord Jesus Christ grant that I may declare these things in such a way that they are pleasing to him, that is, true and for the sanctification of the divine name.

units.la: Fert autem animus, verè & perspicuè ostendere, nos præcipuo Dei Opt. Max. beneficio, id esse assecutos, quod vt ageremus, & vt nobis polliceremur, fecit nostrum & de Controuersia Eucharistica (eorum, in quâ, quorum studium veri & caritatis Dominus Deus noster hoc tempore explorat, quasi quodam Lydio lapide) & de iis, qui à nobis non nihil dissident, iudicium.
units.tr: Moreover, I am pleased to show truly and clearly that we have obtained, by the special benefit of God Most Good and Most Great, that which he has given us the will to do and the promise to undertake: our own judgement both on the controversy over the Eucharist (in which our God explores at this time the zeal for truth and charity of those who are concerned, as with a kind of touchstone) and on those who differ somewhat from us.

units.la: Qui enim optima conscientia, id vnum agunt, vt non modò veritas doctrinæ syncerè de Cœna Domini tum euidenter demonstretur, tum perspicuè illustretur: sed etiam vt (etiam aduersariorum voce & factis) diluantur sinistra præiudicia, quibus illa, tanquam nigris notis, immerito & inhumanissimè aspergitur; ij, siquidem istud obtineant, finem suum, qui rei vltimum optimumque est; &, vt Augustinus ait, opus laudabile reddit, assequuti sunt.
units.tr: For those who, with the best conscience, aim at this one thing, namely that the truth of the doctrine of the Lord's Supper be not only sincerely demonstrated and clearly illustrated, but also that (even by the voice and deeds of our opponents) the sinister prejudices with which it is undeservedly and most inhumanely smeared, as with black marks, be washed away: if they attain this, they have reached their goal, which is the final and best goal of the matter; and, as Augustine says, they make the work praiseworthy.

units.la: Magnas autem toto pectore gratias habeo, Filio Dei Domino nostro Iesu Christo, Agonothetæ & Brabeutæ nostri agminis & certaminis, quòd inæstimabili ipsius beneficio, id ipsum concessum nobis fuit, & reuera illustre exemplum nobis exhibitum, commemorabilis sententiæ, viri bonorum amore & malorum odio clarissimi Philippi Me-lanchthonis. Cuncta Dei opera fiunt per media contraria, quando non ipsi solùm, prout dedit Dominus, causam egimus nostram: sed etiam pars aduersa, id est, conserui illi nostri, qui non per omnia idem de Eucharistia sentiunt, quod nos, contulerunt non parum ad nostræ causæ bonitatem & euidentiam con-firmandam & illustrandam, id quod cordatos & eruditos homines, qui octo nostris congressibus inter-fuerunt, & cum iudicio omnia audierunt, facile ani-maduertisse, mihi in Domino meo Iesu Christo persuadeo.
units.tr: I give great thanks with my whole heart to the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, the president and prize-giver of our host and contest, that by his inestimable benefit this very thing has been granted to us, and that a truly illustrious example has been set before us of that memorable saying of the most famous Philip Melanchthon, a man renowned for his love of good men and his hatred of the wicked: All the works of God are done through contrary means. For not only have we ourselves pleaded our cause, as the Lord gave us the ability, but the opposing side, that is, those fellow-servants of ours who do not hold all the same views on the Eucharist as we do, have contributed not a little to confirming and illustrating the goodness and clarity of our cause. I am persuaded in my Lord Jesus Christ that wise and learned men, who attended our eight encounters and heard everything with judgement, have easily perceived this.

units.la: ETenim, si nos, qui quod corde credimus ad iu-stitiam, id ore profitemur ad salutem, sapiens aesti-mator, intueatur; et, quid a nobis institutum, di-ctum & præstitum sit, candide [illegible, ~10 letters] consideret, etiam nobis imposterum sacro silentio utentibus, deprehendet, ista, quæ iam numero perstringemus, omnia.
units.tr: For if a wise judge considers us, who with the heart believe unto righteousness and with the mouth confess unto salvation, and carefully considers what has been undertaken, said and done by us, he will discover that all these things, which we now briefly touch upon, are so, even though we henceforth keep a sacred silence.

units.la: I. Optima conscientia nos ad optimæ nostræ causæ iustam defensionem accessisse, tum ut sacræ nostræ vocationi & professioni minimè deessemus, tum ut religiosissimæ Illustrissimi Principis (Eccle-siæ tranquillitatis & veritatis doctrinæ cœlestis amantissimi) voluntati, ita ut nos decebat, satisface-remus. De me autem (ut istud [illegible, ~9 letters] profitear) ne-quaquam id dici potest, quod est in Proverbio: Viro Lydo negocium non erat, itaq; foras profectus emit quod ageret. Non enim obscurum est iis, qui vitæ meæ & occupationum, addo & genij & ingenij mei rationes perspectas habet: esse mihi domi in patria Academia quod publici boni ergò, divinas profitendo literas, agam. Vocatus autem ab Illustris: Principe, nō sine commeatu & consensu inclyti mei Magistratus Sa-pientissimi, inquam, celeberrimæ Basiliensis Civi-tatis Senat' ⸗, huc accessi, non ut ἀσύντακτον[?] Periclem, in laudatissima Heydelbergensi Academia agerem; qui nec αὐτοσχεδιάζειν τὰ δέοντα, nec si velim (dicendi facultate non ita magna præditus) possim fulguran-do, tonando & permiscendo, res crudas commoue-re, ut Hippocratis utar verbo. Nunquam fui ἀλλοτριο-[?] ἐπισκόπῳ[?], nec ero unquā, ita mihi dexter perpetuō assit Dominus meus Jesus Christus; qui cum ab ado-lescentia mea jugum ipsius me ferre voluerit, hoc mihi jam pridem persuasit, ut ipsi & per gloriam & per ignominiam servire, mihi sit propositum. Quod tamen Communionis Sanctorum, publicæq; causa-sæ rationem me habere, pietas ipsa juberet, Præsidis in hac disputatione partes, ab Illustrissimo Princi-pe, & Sapientissimis Dominis Consiliarijs, mihi de-mandatas, licet onus viribus meis impar, & multò maius, quàm præviderâm, mihi passus sum imponi: plus enim vero tribuens & bonitati nostræ causæ, & gravissimorum hominum judicio, quàm & aliorum præjudiciis, quæ mihi meditata jam erant omnia, & meæ τῇ εὐθυμίᾳ, quæ mihi occinebat beati Augusti-ni dictum: Tutior est conditio audientis, quàm dicen-tis. Unus itaque, hospes, libris destitutus, excepi tela eorum, qui scriptis, librorum adparatu instru-cti, & cives huius loci, socia jungentes consilia & Theologica arma, non sine applausoribus suis acce-debant; animis, ut sæpiculè sensi, nonnihil commo-tis; tis; quo nomine mihi ab omni vehementia & acri-monia constanter abstinendum esse duxi, nec me, ut scitis omnes, vel sævis dictis ullis, passus sum con-citari: cuius propositi me quidem non pœnitebit unquam.
units.tr: I. We came to the just defence of our excellent cause with the best conscience, both so that we might not fail our sacred calling and profession, and so that we might satisfy, as was fitting for us, the most religious will of the Illustrious Prince, who loves the tranquillity of the Church and the doctrine of heavenly truth. As for myself (to profess this), it cannot by any means be said of me what the proverb says: "The Lydian had no business, so he went abroad and bought something to do." For it is not unknown to those who have a clear view of my life and occupations, and I add of my disposition and talent, that I have at home, in my native academy, work to do, teaching divine letters for the public good. But I was called by the Illustrious Prince, and came here not without leave and consent of my distinguished and most wise magistracy, I say, of the famous Senate of the city of Basel. I did not come to Heidelberg, the most praised academy, to act as an unprepared Pericles, one who could neither improvise what was needed, nor, even if I wished (not being endowed with a great power of speech), move crude matters by lightning, thunder and confusion, to use the word of Hippocrates. I have never been a bishop of another's flock, nor ever shall be, so may my Lord Jesus Christ stand always at my right hand. He who wished me to bear his yoke from my youth long ago persuaded me that it is my purpose to serve him both through glory and through disgrace. Yet the duty of Communion of the Saints and of the public cause itself bade me take account of it; the role of president in this disputation, entrusted to me by the Illustrious Prince and the most wise Lords Councillors, I bore, though the burden was unequal to my strength and far greater than I had foreseen. For I placed more trust in the goodness of our cause and in the judgement of the most serious men than in the prejudices of others; and my own cheerfulness, which sang to me the saying of the blessed Augustine: The condition of the listener is safer than that of the speaker. So, a stranger and without books, I received the darts of those who came forward, equipped with writings and a store of books, and who, joining their counsels and theological weapons with the citizens of this place, approached not without their supporters; their minds, as I often perceived, were somewhat stirred. For this reason I judged that I must steadfastly abstain from all vehemence and sharpness, and, as you all know, I did not allow myself to be provoked by any savage words. I shall certainly never regret this resolve.

units.la: II. Propositas autem esse Theses, perspicuè vereque, ac citra aliorum odiosam reprehensionem aut insectationem scriptas, res ipsa testatur. Secutus autem sum methodum Tabellæ, quæ de Controver-sia Eucharistica in gratiam heroicorum & nobilissimorum quorundam Iuvenum non ita pridem scripta: & à magni nominis viro alibi [illegible, ~8 letters], absente auctore, bono consilio, edita est. Illud autem certò scio, auctori Tabellæ, neque per febrim neque per somnium unquam in mentem venisse, deliramentum impium stolidumque, quod fingit Cœnæ Do-minicæ Institutionem, ad τὸν λόγον[?] restringendam esse, quum illa toti Emmanuelis Iesu Christi perso-næ accepta sit ferenda. Ut autem mihi nequaquam unquam visum est, Antagonistarum ullis, seu simpli-cibus seu coniunctis verbis, simulandi nescio cuius non veri consensus gratia, uti: Sed potius cum disertissimis Oratoribus, Apostolis & Evangelistis: ac cum tota Antiquitate Ecclesiastica, & sentire & loqui: Sic existimavi initio ea, de quibus cæteroquin disidentibus convenit, ordinè & perspicuè & fide optima recitanda, ut ostenderem à Cœna Domini-ca nequaquam Christum Dominum, sine quo nihil sanctum, nihil salutare est, à nobis excludi; aut veritatē Institutionis verborum, Christique Iesu fidem in pactis seruandis, omnipotentiam aut præsentiam, qua toti Ecclesiastico Ministerio à se instituto semper & vbique gentium adest, in dubium scelerate à quoquam nostrum vocari: deinde, in quo cardine controuersia versetur: postremò quibus vtraq; pars fundamentis nitatur, quàm sit manifesta & inui-cta veritas & bonitas nostræ causæ: hæc tria, inquam, sic mihi exponenda duxi, vt partem alteram haud fe-cus interim tractarem, quàm me ipsum ab ea cupi-am officiosè tractari & haberi.
units.tr: II. That the Theses have been set out clearly and truthfully, and written without hateful censure or attack on others, the thing itself bears witness. I followed the method of a Tabella on the Eucharistic controversy, written not long ago for the benefit of certain noble and distinguished young men, and published elsewhere, with the author absent, by a man of great name [illegible, ~8 letters], on good advice. Yet I know for certain that it never came into the mind of the author, either in fever or in dream, to give the impious and foolish delirium that would restrict the institution of the Lord's Supper to the Word [τὸν λόγον], when it ought rightly to be ascribed to the whole person of Emmanuel Jesus Christ. But as it never seemed right to me to use any words, simple or compound, of my opponents, in order to feign some agreement that is not real, but rather to speak and think with the most eloquent orators, the Apostles and Evangelists, and with the whole ecclesiastical antiquity, so I judged that at the start those matters on which the disagreeing parties otherwise agree should be recited in order, clearly, and in the best faith, so that I might show that Christ the Lord, without whom nothing is holy and nothing saving, is by no means shut out by us from the Lord's Supper; nor that anyone among us wickedly calls into doubt the truth of the institution of the words, the faith of Christ Jesus in keeping his covenants, or his omnipotence and presence, by which he is always and everywhere present to the whole ecclesiastical ministry instituted by himself among the nations. Then, I say, I judged that these three things should be set out for me: in what the point of the controversy turns; and finally on what foundations each side rests, and how manifest and unconquered is the truth and goodness of our cause. And I thought it right to handle the other side meanwhile no less courteously than I would wish myself to be handled and held.

units.la: III. Responsum est etiam ad Argumenta (vt amanter ea sic vocem, quando parti alteri talia esse videntur) placidè: & cum Præsidis munere mihi esset defungendum, necesse habui declarare nonnulla. Verbi gratia Enunciationem istam: Totus Christus est vbique, sed non totum Christi, exposui verbis Damasceni, qui ait: τὸ μὲν ὅλον, φύσεως ἐστὶ πρακτικόν[?], τὸ δὲ ὅλον ὑποστάσεως[?]. Totum denotat naturam, totum autem personam. Professus sum me agnoscere, Christum qua homo est, vbique esse: sed vt beatus Cyrillus ait, καθ᾽ ἄλλο[?] ἢ ἄλλο[?]: quando humanitas Christi vbique est, non in se ipsa, sed in alio, vt dixit Leo Romanus Episcopus. Nihil à me retractatum est, nihil quod dextera datum fuit, sinistra vnquam eripui: sed vitandæ ambiguitatis gratia, necessarias expositiones vocum, instituì, vt intelligentes omnes facilè animaduerterunt.
units.tr: III. Replies were also made, calmly, to the arguments (as I call them kindly, since they seem to be such to the other party), and since I had to discharge the office of the chairman, I was obliged to declare some points. For example, I explained that statement: The whole Christ is everywhere, but not the whole of Christ, in the words of Damascene, who says: the whole [τὸ μὲν ὅλον] belongs to nature as active, and the whole to hypostasis. Whole denotes nature, but whole denotes person. I professed that I acknowledge Christ, as man, to be everywhere; but, as the blessed Cyril says, not in one way or another [καθ᾽ ἄλλο ἢ ἄλλο]: since the humanity of Christ is everywhere, not in itself, but in another, as Leo, bishop of Rome, said. Nothing has been retracted by me, nothing that I gave with the right hand have I ever snatched back with the left; but for the sake of avoiding ambiguity I set out the necessary explanations of the terms, as all who understood readily observed.

units.la: Quam verò facilè fuerit, ad obiectiones Adversariorum, mediocriter exercitato, respondere, vel sola præcipuarum recensio satis ostendit.
units.tr: How easily it would be, for a moderately practised man, to answer the objections of the adversaries, the mere listing of the principal ones shows well enough.

units.la: I. Non est tropus in subiecto & prædicato huius Enunciationis: Panis est corpus Christi. Ergo nul Ius[?] inest tropus. Quasi verò non sit in genere attri-butionis sacramentalis, nec multa de toto verè dici possint, quæ de parte aliqua non ita non prædicantur.
units.tr: I. There is no trope in the subject and predicate of this statement: The bread is the body of Christ. Therefore no trope is present. As if there were not one in the kind of sacramental attribution, nor could many things be truly said of the whole that are not, in a certain way, not predicated of some part.

units.la: 2. Filij Dei appellatio solùm τὸν λόγον[?] denotat. Igitur qui ait Coenam Domini à Filio Dei institutā, negat eandem ab Immanuele & Homine Christo in-stitutam. O Carneadeum acumen: & strenuam in Antecedente petitionem principij?
units.tr: 2. The appellation Son of God denotes only the Word [τὸν λόγον]. Therefore whoever says that the Lord's Supper was instituted by the Son of God denies that it was instituted by Immanuel and the man Christ. O Carneadean keenness! And a vigorous begging of the question in the antecedent?

units.la: 3. Patres manducārunt tantùm ἐνέργειαν[?] corporis Christi, quod nondum actu existebat. Non ergo ita vt nos viuificam Christi carnem comederunt.
units.tr: 3. The Fathers ate only the power [ἐνέργειαν] of the body of Christ, which did not yet actually exist. Therefore they did not eat Christ's flesh as life-giving as we do.

units.la: Quasi ἐνέργεια[?] aliqua sit eius rei, quæ nullo modo extat in natura rerum? Non enim illis libet nobiscum credere, carnem Christi, quæ ordine naturæ nondum erat Patrum inquam ætate, & coram Deo promittēte, & ratione fidei, quæ facit vt exstent quæ sperantur, & est ἐλέγχῳ[?] eorum quæ non videntur, Patribus neutiquam defuisse, quando Iesus Christus heri & hodie idem est & in secula.
units.tr: As if there were some power [ἐνέργεια] of a thing that in no way exists in the nature of things? For they are not willing to believe with us that the flesh of Christ, which in the order of nature did not yet exist in the age of the Fathers, I say, and in God promising, and by the reason of faith, which makes things hoped for to exist and is the proof [ἐλέγχῳ] of things not seen, was by no means lacking to the Fathers, since Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.

units.la: 4. Sacramenta proprie dicta, habent institutio-nem divinam, signum, rem signatam, effectum: vt etiam D. Beza scribit.
units.tr: 4. Sacraments properly so called have a divine institution, a sign, a thing signified, and an effect, as Beza also writes.

units.la: Hæc autem de Agno Paschali & de Manna dici nequeunt.
units.tr: But these things cannot be said of the Passover lamb or of the manna.

units.la: Quare hæc duo inter propriè dicta Sacramenta referri nequeunt.
units.tr: Therefore these two cannot be counted among sacraments properly so called.

units.la: 5. In qua propositione corporis Christi vocabulum, de vero & essentiali ipsius corpore dicitur, ea τῷ ῥήματι[?] accipienda est.
units.tr: 5. In which proposition the word body of Christ is said of his true and essential body itself, it must be taken in that sense [τῷ ῥήματι].

units.la: Atqui in propositione: Hoc est Corpus meum, ita sumitur Corporis vocabulum. Ergò &c.
units.tr: But in the proposition: This is my body, the word body is taken in this way. Therefore etc.

units.la: 6 Quòd (verè & propriè loquendo) manduca‐tur,id ore manducatur. Atqui Christi corpus (pro‐priè loquêdo)manducatur. Igitur ore manducatur.
units.tr: 6. What is eaten (speaking truly and properly) is eaten by the mouth. But the body of Christ is eaten (speaking properly). Therefore it is eaten by the mouth.

units.la: 7 Augustinus dicit etiam Infidelem totum Sa‐cramentum percipere. Igitur infidelis manducat Christi carnem.
units.tr: 7. Augustine says that even the unbeliever receives the whole sacrament. Therefore the unbeliever eats the flesh of Christ.

units.la: Quasi verò Augustinus non sit synecdochicè lo‐cutus? Omitto aliorum Sophismatum recensionem. Vt enim leonem ex vnguibus: sic exijs quę dixi,&cę‐tera leptologemata, & eos quibus illa placent, pru‐dens æstimator facilè agnoscet & dijudicabit.
units.tr: As if Augustine had not spoken by synecdoche? I pass over the enumeration of other sophisms. For as one knows the lion from its claws, so from what I have said, and the other trifling word-games, and those who are pleased with them, a prudent judge will readily recognise and discern.

units.la: IIII. Dixi vera & consentanea per totam Disputationem, quia non respexi ad latissimos humana‐rum doctrinarum, seu potius opinionum, Septen‐triones, sed ad Cynosurâ verbi Dei, quæ nequaquam fallit. Ideò, quicquid nonnulli (diserti sui in Theolo‐gia profectus patroni) falsò dictitent & spargant, de meo silentio, quo me nunquam in hac disputatione vsum, oês quotquot adfuerunt, probè nouerunt: &, de nõ Entis efficacitate cõcessa (quâ ab hominibus, qui se Theologos dici cupiunt, in quæstione de Iesv Christo, qui Est, qui Erat, & qui Venturus est, mihi obiectâ esse, sapientes homines quibus animis audi‐turos, iudicatis?) me quidem, nec dictorum meo‐rum, nec laborũ, quos sustinui minimè certè vulga‐res, piget aut pœnitet. Ex animo autem, vt verum di‐cam, miseret eorum omnium, qui sibi clauem co‐gnitionis sumunt, & non introeunt, introire autem cupientes prohibent. Veram Christi præsentiam, qua habitat in cordibus nostris per fidem, & nos sibi concorpores efficit, ex toto Euangelio, perspicuè probaui:cum pars altera præsentia corporis Christi in pane ne quidem vnico Scripturæ sanctæ apice, confirmare potuerit. Sacra Symbola Oraliter, ipsam autem Christi carnem per fidem Spiritualiter accipi docui; quum Oralem illam Carnis Christi manducationem, qua sensualiter editur & dentibus teritur, pars altera, non nisi Nicolai Papæ, & Neotericorum suffragatorum eius (quibus recte Scholiastes Iuris Canonici reclamauit) auctoritate, siculno sane præsidio, possit tueri. Pronomen Hoc, in verbis Domini nostri Iesu Christi: Hoc est Corpus meum, de pane intelligi debere ostendi, quando & prius enunciatum fuit, quàm corporis facta esset mentio: & alioquin non disparatum de disparato, sed idem de eo demin epte prædicaretur: & denique Paulus disertè dixit, Panis quem frangimus nonne communio Corporis Christi est? Nihil de eo iam dicam, quod de poculo dicitur, subiecti demonstrandi gratia: Hoc poculum nouum Testamentum in sanguine meo, &c. Magnum equidem argumentum optimæ & sanctissimæ nostræ causæ est, illa omnium eius partium sinceritas καταχμονία, seu consensio, quando verum vero per omnia suauissimè consonat.
units.tr: IIII. I have said true and consistent things throughout the whole Disputation, because I did not look to the most wide-ranging north of human doctrines, or rather opinions, but to the Cynosure of the Word of God, which never deceives. Therefore, whatever certain persons (patrons of their own eloquent progress in theology) falsely keep saying and spreading about my silence, by which I never made use of myself in this disputation, all who were present know well; and as for the concession of the efficacy of non-being (by which, when I was objected to in the question about Jesus Christ, who is, who was, and who is to come, by men who wish to be called theologians, you judge with what minds wise men will hear them?), I for my part am not sorry or repentant of my words, nor of my labours, which I undertook, by no means small. Truly, to speak the truth from the heart, I pity all those who take to themselves the key of knowledge and do not enter, and forbid those who wish to enter. The true presence of Christ, by which he dwells in our hearts through faith and makes us concorporeal with himself, I have clearly proved from the whole Gospel, whereas the other party could not confirm the presence of Christ's body in the bread by so much as a single jot of holy Scripture. I taught that the holy symbols are received orally, but the flesh of Christ itself spiritually through faith; whereas the other party, the oral eating of Christ's flesh, by which it is eaten sensually and ground by the teeth, could defend only by the authority of Pope Nicholas and of his modern supporters (whom the scholiast of canon law rightly opposed), which is surely no help at all. I showed that the pronoun This, in the words of our Lord Jesus Christ: This is my body, must be understood of the bread, since it was stated before the mention of the body was made; otherwise it would not be a disparate predicated of a disparate, but the same thing would be predicated of itself, absurdly; and finally Paul plainly said: The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? I will say nothing further about what is said of the cup, for the sake of the demonstrative subject: This cup is the new testament in my blood, etc. Indeed it is a great argument for the best and most holy cause of ours that there is that sincerity of all its parties, καταχμονία, or agreement, when truth consonates most sweetly with truth in all things.

units.la: V. Contumeliosas voces, quibus tam nonnulli sancti Dei homines, in Iesu Christi sinu iam quiescentes, quàm superstites quidam eximij Dei serui, à parte altera profecti fuerunt: ideo surdis auribus praeteriuimus, quia delectamur, Nazianzeni grauissimis & saluberrimis versibus, quorum hæc sententia est. Si quando contumelia vrit tuum pectus: memento Christi, memeto eius vulnerum. Quota autem portio [?]lo est eorum quae tua caussa tulit Dominus? Ita vel-ut infusa aqua id dilues, quod te urit, & magnopere tibi dolet.
units.tr: V. The abusive words, with which certain holy men of God, now resting in the bosom of Jesus Christ, as well as certain surviving outstanding servants of God, were attacked from the other side, we have therefore passed by with deaf ears, because we are delighted with the most weighty and wholesome verses of Nazianzen, whose sense is this: If ever an insult burns your breast, remember Christ, remember his wounds. How small a portion of what the Lord bore for your sake is that insult! So, as water poured on, dilute what burns you and greatly grieves you.

units.la: VI. Fortassis autem judicio sapientum, peccaui nimia erga interrogantes quosdam lenitate, quae fo-nestra ἀ[?]πλανήσεως & digressionum, ac repetitionum (nihil ut gravius dicā) illis aperuit. Sed ita ingenium meum est, nunquam non, de caritatis praecepto tam sanctè nobis ab ipso Deo praescripto, & de judice nostro ante januam adstante: deque mea imbecil-litate, cogitanti, sentio viscera miserationum commoueri, quando etiam infestum & insolentem Ad-versarium, vel haerere perplexum (sic ut syllogismos in illius gratiam me formare necesse sit) vel sibi ipsi inconsultis dictis, humanitatis & doctrinae laudem, & eruditi hominis personam, coram multis arbitris, eripere, animaduerto. Malui tamen patienter multa ferre, & taedium omne devorare, quàm inflammatus τῇ ἰσχυρογνωμοσύνῃ, & acerbitate dictorum, talionem reponere: & disputationis abrumpendae ansam cuiquam praebere. Non enim ingenij & ubertatis doctrinae (quam in me non magnam agnosco) ostentandae: sed asserendae piae veraeque de Coena Domini nostrae Confessionis gratia, me adesse, functioneque religiosa publici muneris me defungi, per Christi gratiam probè noueram. Fortassis autem morosi quidam Censores, ubi meo exemplo in proscenium aliquando prodierint, & arduam aliquam caussam susceperint tractandam; diuersitatisque ingeniorum gustum perceperint; ac quid ipsorum quoque humeri valeant, fuerint experti, non nihil meis istis studijs & laboribus, æquiores erunt. Audio autem & illud impatienter quendam ferre, quòd à me, hospite in hac Schola, & quorundam in differendo virtutis & vsus ignaro, nominatus, postea tamen conferendi mecum locum non obtinuit; verùm si quis dè is, pro sua modestia, suis scse collegis doctiorem esse non iudicat, hosque causse suæ non defuisse censet: boni consulet, quòd, non vllo nostro consilio, sed collegarum suorum copiosa facundia, eo fuit adductus, tacere vt illi liceret, exemplo Antesignani, (oculi agminis sui) quem scit in harenam non descendisse, sed & tyrones suos, triariorum loco libeter habuisse, eisque rem totam commisisse, sibíque egregiè sanè & comicè cauisse.
units.tr: VI. Perhaps, in the judgment of the wise, I have been too gentle with certain questioners, which has opened the door to digressions, evasions and repetitions (to say nothing harsher). But such is my disposition: whenever I think of the command of charity, so solemnly prescribed to us by God himself, and of the judge standing at our door, and of my own weakness, I feel my heart moved to compassion. Even when I notice that a hostile and insolent opponent is stuck in confusion (so that I must frame syllogisms for his benefit), or that by ill-considered remarks he is losing, before many witnesses, the praise of courtesy and learning and the reputation of a learned man, I have preferred to bear many things patiently and swallow all weariness, rather than, inflamed by obstinacy and bitterness of speech, pay back in kind and give anyone a reason to break off the disputation. For I knew well, by the grace of Christ, that I was present not to display cleverness or the abundance of learning (which I acknowledge I do not have in great measure), but to defend the pious and true Confession of our Lord's Supper, and to discharge a public office with religious duty. Perhaps, however, some peevish critics, once they have come forward on the stage after my example and taken up some difficult cause to treat, and have tasted the variety of talents and found out what their own shoulders can bear, will be somewhat more fair to my studies and labours. I hear, moreover, that a certain man bore it impatiently that he was named by me, a guest in this school and ignorant of the virtue and practice of disputing, yet afterwards did not obtain a place to confer with me. But if someone, in his modesty, does not judge himself more learned than his colleagues, and thinks they did not fail his cause, let him take it kindly that I was led, not by any counsel of ours but by the abundant eloquence of his colleagues, to allow him to keep silent, after the example of the Antesignanus (the eye of his own army), who, as he knows, did not descend into the arena himself but was pleased to keep his recruits in the place of the triarii, and committed the whole matter to them, and took very fine and rather comic care of himself.

units.la: Dixi fide bona, quomodo vt causam nostram ipsi ageremus, Dominus dederit: postulat iam institutì nostri ratio, vt eadem fide & perspicuitate, citra cuiusquam odiosam nomenclaturam, ostendam, quomodo pars altera negocium suum egerit. Enimuero quum plurimum laborauerit, in eodem tamen statu hærens, nostræ interim causæ non parum profecto contulit; vt hic quoque admirabilia Dei iudicia, nos agnoscere, & sanctissimo nostro instituto, ex animo nos gratulari, æquissimum sit.
units.tr: I have said, in good faith, how the Lord has granted us to plead our own cause. The plan of our undertaking now requires that, with the same good faith and clarity, and without any odious naming of anyone, I show how the other side has conducted its business. Indeed, although it has laboured greatly yet remained in the same condition, it has in the meantime contributed not a little to our cause; so it is only fair that we here too acknowledge the wonderful judgments of God and heartily rejoice in our most holy undertaking.

units.la: I. Si enim ἀντιβολίσμον, seu primam velitationem, qua eminus nos adoriedo, ambigua, vbi nulla plane erant secantes, sub quouis lapide Scorpiū quæsiuerunt: & deinde, iustum dissertationis prælium, in quo collatis signis, illorum Sophisticis & nostris Apodicticis, actum fuit, prudenter quispiam consideret: re ipsa deprehendet, illos initio quidem capitum quorundam rundā, de Institutore Cœnæ Domini, de eius præsentia, & de veritate verborū Institutionis, de quibus Controuersia inter pios nulla est, quasi quosdā margines, genuino infixo frustrà cōcutere & lacerare conatos: vt scilicet ἀκρίβειας & circumspectionis admirandam, apud rerum imperitos, famā aucuparentur: deinde verò, vehementer rogatos à nobis, vt si ita serrent eorū animi virefq; cum hasta, cum scuto, ipsam caussæ arcem inuaderent. Ac donec modestè ab illis actum fuit, laude ea à me ornati sunt citra fucum aliquem: quàm illi immodestè postea agendo, sibiipsis absterserunt. Vt nō tam sit, curij meum in laudando candorem, eo nomine ambitiosè allegent, sui videlicet ornādi caussa, quibus ipse postea admonitionis ad modestiam sale, non nihil fui molestus: quam cur sibiipsis eo displiceant nomine, quòd grauitatis Theologicæ propositum mutantes, in reprehensionem, non meam solùm, sed etiam aliorum quorundam prudentium hominum, inciderunt.
units.tr: I. For if someone prudently considers the first skirmish, the preliminary attack in which they assailed us from a distance with ambiguous arguments, where there were plainly no cutting points, and sought a scorpion under every stone, and then the regular battle of disputation, in which the signs were exchanged, their sophistical arguments against our demonstrative ones, he will discover in fact that at first they tried in vain to shake and tear certain marginal points, about the Institutor of the Lord's Supper, about his presence, and about the truth of the words of institution, on which there is no controversy among the pious, as if they were attacking the outworks while the main fortress stood intact. Their purpose was clearly to win a reputation for remarkable precision and caution among those ignorant of such matters. Then, when they were earnestly asked by us, if their spirits and strength allowed it, to attack the very citadel of the cause with spear and shield, they did so. And while they conducted themselves modestly, I honoured them with that praise, without any pretence; but by behaving immodestly afterwards they wiped it away themselves. So let them not now boast ambitiously of my candour in praising them, for the sake of adorning themselves, when I myself was somewhat troublesome to them by warning them, with a touch of salt, toward modesty. Let them rather be displeased with themselves for this reason: that, changing the purpose of theological seriousness, they fell into reproof, not only of me but also of certain other prudent men.

units.la: EX Sophisticis itaque Catapultis & machinis, tela & phalaricæ plumbeæ, in Veritatis adamantinam petram eiaculatæ & contorte sunt, tanto enimuerò conatu, vt amissa acie, obtusa relaberentur.
units.tr: So from the sophistical catapults and machines, darts and leaden fire-bolts were hurled and hurled again against the adamantine rock of the truth, with such effort that, their edge lost, they rebounded blunted.

units.la: Operæ pretium autem fuerit & illud scire, quos fines illi sibi proposuerint, & quę tandem capita dostrinæ obtinere conati sint. Primum erat, etiam infideles, Cœna Domini vtentes manducare, & quidem ore corporis, sanctissimum illud Iesu Christi Corpus; sed tamen ad iudiciū. Atqui nec in illorum gratiam instituta est Cœna: & corpus Christi man-ducatum, vitam; spretum & abiectum, mortem (sed hoc accidentaliter, non participationis, sed priuationis respectu) operatur. Secundum, sanctissimos Deoq; charissimos Patres, non manducasse corpus Christi, sed tantùm eius ἐνέργειαν[?]: quasi verò deterior olim fuerit Patrum conditio, quàm hoc tempore (opinione illorum) infidelium est, vel etiam vis viui-ficandi à participatione corporis Christi seiungi posset: vel denique Christus Iudicis munere fungi nequeat, erga infideles, nisi hi corpus illius Oraliter prius manducent; quo posito, sequitur non iudicandos eos infideles, qui sacra Cœna nunquam vtuntur. Tertium, Oraliter non minus Christi carnem, quàm panem in sacra Cœna edi. Atqui implicat contradictionem, si quis dicat, corpus Christi localiter non adesse, corporaliter adesse; oraliter & supernaturaliter manducari. Quartum, Scriptum in Verbis Cœnæ Domini sequendum: quo posito Transubstantiatio Papistica potius sequetur, quàm Cardinalis Cameracensis delirium, videlicet Consubstantiatio, seu præsentia corporis Christi ad locum panis. Talia autem fuisse aduersæ partis Sophistica le-ptologemata, quales fuerunt, Theses, quas defendendas susceperunt, quis homo prudens miretur, cum similes habeant labra lactucas?
units.tr: It will also be worth knowing what ends they set for themselves, and what heads of doctrine they tried to hold. The first was that even unbelievers, using the Lord's Supper, eat, indeed with the mouth of the body, that most holy Body of Jesus Christ, but unto judgment. Yet the Supper was not instituted for their sake, and the body of Christ eaten produces life, but when despised and rejected it produces death (though this happens incidentally, with respect not to participation but to deprivation). The second was that the most holy and most dear to God Fathers did not eat the body of Christ, but only its energy; as if the condition of the Fathers was once worse than that of unbelievers at this time (in their opinion), or as if the power of quickening could be separated from participation in the body of Christ, or finally as if Christ could not perform the office of Judge toward unbelievers unless they first eat his body orally. Given this, it follows that those unbelievers who never use the holy Supper are not to be judged. The third was that in the Words of the Lord's Supper the flesh of Christ is eaten orally no less than the bread. Yet it implies a contradiction if someone says that the body of Christ is not present locally, yet is present bodily, and is eaten orally and supernaturally. The fourth was that the Scripture is to be followed in the words of the Lord's Supper; given this, the Papistical transubstantiation would follow rather than the delirium of the Cardinal of Cambrai, namely consubstantiation, or the presence of the body of Christ at the place of the bread. That such were the sophistical quibbles of the opposing side, such as were the theses they undertook to defend, why should any sensible man be surprised, since their lips have lettuces of the same kind?

units.la: 2. Iam quum iidem, erroribus illis, alios insuper nouos, & in Ecclesia nunquam antea auditos, addi-derint; & quidem eiusmodi, vt mihi quidè dubium non sit, etiam præceptores istorum interrogantium, doctos & exercitatos homines, nunquam eos esse approbaapprobaturos: quis non videat, ipsos sibi & caussæ suæ male consuluisse? Quis vnquam in Ecclesia aut Schola Christiana audiuit hanc κενοφωνίαν: Filij Dei appellatio restringenda est ad λόγον: quum Pater æternus cœlitus clamauerit, dicens: Hic est Filius meus dilectus, in quo acquiesco? Item, quum toties in Scripturis, etiā Filij appellatio, κατ' ἐξοχὴν sumta, totam Immanuelis, veri Dei & veri Hominis, personam designet? Quis vnquam fando audiuit, è proprie dictorum Sacramentorum Albo expungendum esse Agnum Paschalem & Mannam? Paulus Magistro suo Iesu Christo subscribens, inter proprie dicta Sacramenta ea refert, & cum nostris illa confert, ὁ ζητῶν[?] ex Interrogantibus negat: vtri, quæso vos Opt. Auditores, credemus? Equidem Apostolo malim ipse idem habere. Negauit idem fortiter, Cordis Circumcisionem esse rem Sacramenti, in Circumcisione: & identidem Fœdus rem Sacramenti esse contendit, cum hoc vt totum, cætera complectatur. Fortiter affirmauit, Patres nec promissionē habuisse nec mandatum de carne Christi manducanda: quum Paulus dicat: Omnes eandem escam spiritualem ederunt: & omnes eundem potum spiritualem biberunt, Bibebant enim ex sequente spirituali Petra. Petra autem erat Christus. 1. Corint. 10. Capite. versu 3. & 4. Negauit etiam idem verba Institutionis Cœnæ Dominicæ, fidei conditionem requirere: quasi vero non sint verba promissionis gratiæ: vt piè monet Augustanæ Confessionis Apologia. Dixit quidam ex aduersa parte, satis profectò Cathedraliter, Non extare apud Mosen, Gen. 17. Enunciationem, Circumcisio est fœdus. Quasi vero eam non stolidus lector, ex versib 10. & 11. colligere ne-queat: quum ita habeant verba: Hoc est pactum meum quod obseruabitis inter me & vos, atq; inter semen tuum post te, ut circumcidatur in vobis omnis masculus. Circumcidetis vero carnem praeputij vestri, eritque signum pacti inter me & vos? Pollicitus est idem ostensurum se, Regulam de Sacramentalibus locutionibus, quas Figuratas nuncupamus, in quibus signo quidem vel nomen rei signatæ, vel huius effectum: signato autem, vel signi nomen vel huius effectum tribuitur, auream non esse (Sic eam ipsemet appellaueram) sed vix esse plumbeam, & nec veram, nec ullius precij. Idem, quum dixissem, Praedica-tionum de Filio Dei alias esse proprias, figuratas ali-as: ac has ad tropum ἀντιστροφῶς[?] & synechdochen spe-ctare, ad proprias reuocari posse: exclamans admo-dum zelose: Ergo tropicum Christum facis: ergo Deitatem illius cum Arrianis in dubium vocas. Mal-lebat, homo acutus, dicere, inusitatas esse: non interim videns quonam (eodem modo, si libuisset, quo ille me argumentante) ei res euasura esset. Saepius autem animadverti, & Sacramentales, & eas quæ de Filio Dei in Scripturis sanctis occurrunt, praedicationes, nimis inusitatas esse quibusdam Rabbinis: quibus videlicet æque ut Ecclesiasticum dicendi genus, & usitatę sunt & notæ. Ecclesiæ me miseret, quæ tales habet Hierophantas, quos certè non puduit in am-plissimorum & grauissimorum virorum corona, Syl-logismos mihi exigenti, respondere: Quorsum opus est Syllogismis aut rationibus? Vt iam de eo nihil dicam, quòd mihi neganti lemma aliquod in ipsorum ar-gutijs, sæpè responsum fuit: Probatu.
units.tr: 2. Now, since these same men, in addition to those errors, have added other new ones never before heard in the Church, and of such a kind that I have no doubt that even the teachers of those questioners, learned and experienced men, would never approve them, who does not see that they have ill served themselves and their cause? Who has ever heard in the Church or in a Christian school this empty talk: that the appellation Son of God must be restricted to the Word, since the eternal Father cried out from heaven, saying: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased"? Likewise, since so often in the Scriptures even the appellation Son, taken absolutely, designates the whole person of Immanuel, true God and true man? Who has ever heard it said that the Paschal Lamb and the Manna must be struck from the list of the properly so-called sacraments? Paul, subscribing to his Master Jesus Christ, counts those among the properly so-called sacraments and compares them with ours; the questioners deny it. Whom, I ask you, most excellent hearers, shall we believe? For my part I would rather have the Apostle himself. The same men stoutly denied that the circumcision of the heart is the thing of the sacrament in circumcision, and repeatedly contended that the covenant is the thing of the sacrament, with this as the whole, embracing the rest. They stoutly affirmed that the Fathers had neither the promise nor the command concerning eating the flesh of Christ, though Paul says: "All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink; for they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ" (1 Cor. 10, verses 3 and 4). The same men also denied that the words of institution of the Lord's Supper require the condition of faith, as if they were not words of the promise of grace, as the Apology of the Augsburg Confession piously reminds us. One man on the other side said, quite pontifically, that the statement "Circumcision is the covenant" is not found in Moses, Gen. 17. As if a foolish reader could not gather it from verses 10 and 11, where the words are: "This is my covenant, which you shall keep between me and you and your seed after you: every male among you shall be circumcised. And you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you." The same man promised to show that the rule about sacramental locutions, which we call figurative, in which the name of the thing signified is given to the sign, or its effect, and the name or effect of the sign is given to the thing signified, is not golden (as I myself had called it), but scarcely even leaden, and neither true nor of any worth. The same man, when I had said that predications concerning the Son of God are some proper and some figurative, and that these refer to the trope of antistrophe and synecdoche and can be reduced to proper ones, exclaimed very zealously: "So you make Christ a figure! So you call his divinity into doubt, along with the Arians!" The clever man would rather have said they were unusual, not seeing where the matter would end up, in the same way (if he had wished) that he was reasoned with by me. I have often observed, moreover, that both sacramental predications and those concerning the Son of God that occur in the holy Scriptures are too unusual for certain rabbis, to whom, just as the ecclesiastical mode of speech, the other kind is customary and familiar. I pity the Church, which has such hierophants, who were not ashamed, in the crown of the most distinguished and most serious men, when I asked for syllogisms, to answer: "Why is there any need of syllogisms or reasons?" Not to mention that when I denied some premise, a reply was often made in their subtleties: "Prove it."

units.la: Quid talia dicenti, aliud respondeas, quàm quod mihi illa audienti tum dictavit charitas: Utinam mihi priuatim ista diceres, sicut silentio tegi possent, nec coram tot tantisque arbitris & testibus, tuæ personæ parum consuleres? Anne autem Prophetarum & Apostolorum loquendi rationem, toti eruditæ pieque Antiquitati ignotam fuisse, aut ab hac depravatam esse putabimus? Idem, quum Sacramenta-lem esse prædicationem in Verbis Pauli: Petra erat Christus, dixissem, allegato etiam Augustini ὁμοιοφ-φ[?] dicto ex Epist. 102. non sine Sardonio risu, illud negans, Quot igitur, ait, tandem Sacramenta constituis? Hæc scilicet homini (Antiquitatis Ecclesiasticæ opor-taneorum sacrorum Mystagogo) ideo dicenda erant, ut, si Deo placet, ex diversis Patrum dictis, quæ docent, Corpus Christi ore percipi, colligeret, oralem illam carnis Christi manducationem? Non enim intelligebat Phrasi Sacramentali, effectum signi, signa-to tribui. Metonymiam tandem agnoscebat in di-cto. Petra erat Christus; in verbis Cœnæ non agno-scebat Metonymiam, ne Tropicum Corpus Christi statuere videretur. Erat sane ἀληθ[?]ς ἀ[?]. Scilicet omne id tropicè tantum, non autem revera est, de quo exstant, non proprię solùm, sed etiam translatæ dicendi formulæ? Simile fuit quondam eius viri acumen, qui negans verbis illis, Hoc est Corpus meum, tropum inesse: interim quiddam τροπικῶς[?], seu tropo similimum inesse ingenuè fatebatur.
units.tr: What answer can you give to someone who says such things, other than what charity dictated to me as I listened to him then: "I wish you had said these things to me privately, where they could be kept quiet, and had not, before so many and such important judges and witnesses, done less than well for your own reputation"? But shall we suppose that the manner of speaking used by the Prophets and Apostles was unknown to all learned and devout antiquity, or that antiquity corrupted it? When I said that the preaching in Paul's words, "The rock was Christ," was sacramental, and cited also Augustine's similar saying from Epistle 102, he denied it with a sardonic laugh: "How many sacraments, then, do you set up?" Was this man (a mystagogue of the sacred rites of ancient Church practice) really to be told this so that, if God pleases, he might gather from the various sayings of the Fathers, which teach that the body of Christ is received by the mouth, that oral manducation of the flesh of Christ? For he did not understand that in sacramental phrasing the effect is attributed to the sign, and the thing signified. Finally, he recognised a metonymy in the saying "The rock was Christ," but in the words of the Supper he did not recognise a metonymy, lest he seem to posit a tropical body of Christ. Certainly this was a true [ἀληθής] ... Surely everything of which there exist forms of speech, not only proper but also figurative, is really only figurative? The keenness of that man was once similar, who, denying that a trope lies in those words, "This is my body," frankly admitted that something tropical, or very like a trope, was present.

units.la: Quum dicerem, Baptismum dici lauacrum regenerationis, ibi idem ille, Baptismi voce & signum & signatum existimans indicari, nec homonymiæ vocis Baptismi, nec dicti Petri, Baptismus nos seruat, non quo carnis sordes abijciuntur, &c. ullam habuit rationem.
units.tr: When I said that Baptism is called the washing of regeneration, that same man, thinking that both the sign and the thing signified were indicated by the word Baptism, took no account of the equivocation of the word Baptism, nor of Peter's saying, "Baptism saves us, not because the filth of the flesh is put away," etc.

units.la: Omitto, (ut honori alieno parcam: non nisi atroce προκαταληπτικὴ[?] causa copulsus, ea prolaturus in lucem) alia absurda ψευδοσφήματα[?]; nam & ista, (licet ij[?], qui ad Catadupa prodigiosi sui dogmatis & anathematismorum hactenus versati, nobis gladiatorio animo sese opposuerunt, ea quæ dixi, confidentissime protulerunt) non sine commiseratione & crebris gemitibus, repeto. Dei vero iudicia veneror & agnosco, eumque oro, ut nobis det veritatem constanter profiteri & tueri: ac ut cæteros quoque in veritatis viam deducat.
units.tr: I omit (so as not to spare another's honour, and I would bring these things to light only compelled by a grave cause) other absurd false statements; for these also (although those who, hitherto busy at Catadupa with their prodigious dogma and anathemas, set themselves against us with gladiatorial spirit, most confidently put forward what I have said) I repeat not without pity and frequent groans. But I revere and acknowledge the judgments of God, and pray to Him that He give us to profess and defend the truth constantly, and that He lead the rest also into the way of truth.

units.la: III. Porro, quum ipsimet Domini interrogantes adducerent & probarent quædam illustria de Cœna Domini dicta, Ioannis Caluini, p. m. & V.Cl. Theodori Bezæ, amici mei optimi, eaque toti Auditorio prælegerent, non semel, sed iterum: An non ipsimet testatum fecerunt, atrocem nostris doctoribus & pastoribus iniuriam fieri, quando apud imperitam multitudinem, non equidem sine stentoreis clamoribus, traducuntur, quasi in Cœna nihil aliud agnoscant, præterquam nuda, & μνημονευτικὰ[?] tantum signa efficaciæ ac meritorum; non etiam ipsius viuificæ Carnis Christi communionem statuant? Recte equidem Aristoteles pronunciauit, eam laudem magnificiendam esse, quam virtutis manifesta documenta, etiam hostibus extorquent. Debemus ergo Dominis Interrogantibus aliquam gratiam, quod ne quidem rogati, honorarios prœcones innocentiæ nostræ & sincerę confessionis nostræ, eo pacto egerunt: ac vt eadem fidelia duos dealbarent parietes, Hierophantis (qui de nudis Symbolis vitili-gationem nobis intendunt) ora obstruxerunt, quā-do vident Dominum Bezam, etiam illis attestantibus, tam perspicuè docuisse & docere, In Sacra Domini nostri Iesu Christi Cœna, primùm signa Sacramentalia, panem videlicet, vinumque Domini; deinde rem Sacramenti nimirum Corpus Domini pro nobis traditum, Sanguinem Domini pro nobis fusum: postremò efficaciam fructumque Spiritualem, perse ex toto corde agnoscere, constanterque & perspicuè profiteri.
units.tr: III. Further, when the very questioners of the Lords themselves brought forward and proved certain illustrious sayings about the Lord's Supper of John Calvin, of blessed memory, and of the most distinguished Theodore Beza, my best friend, and read them aloud to the whole audience, not once but again: did they not themselves attest that an atrocious injury is done to our teachers and ministers, when they are misrepresented before an unlearned crowd, not without stentorian shouts, as if they recognised in the Supper nothing but bare signs of efficacy and merits, serving only for remembrance, and did not also posit communion with the life-giving flesh of Christ itself? Aristotle rightly pronounced that that praise is to be magnified which even enemies extort from the plain evidence of virtue. We owe therefore some thanks to the questioning Lords, that, though not asked, they acted as honorary heralds of our innocence and of our sincere confession in this way: and that, as the same faithful pair whitewash two walls, they stopped the mouths of the hierophants (who bring against us the charge of bare symbols) when they saw that Lord Beza, even with their attestation, had taught and still teaches so clearly, and openly professes and constantly acknowledges, that in the holy Supper of our Lord Jesus Christ, first, the sacramental signs, namely the bread and the wine of the Lord; then the thing of the sacrament, namely the body of the Lord given for us and the blood of the Lord shed for us; and finally the spiritual efficacy and fruit, are present, with the whole heart.

units.la: IIII. Illud autem, quàm magnum sanctissimæ nostræ causæ argumentum fuit, quòd quum pars aduersa, nunquam antehac, dum adsuimus, Dispu-tatione instituta, nobis argumenta nostra adducen-di copiam fecerit: quod tamen professionis eorum ratio dictabat & postulabat: sed octies[?] nobiscum cō-gressa, suam causam summis suis viribus egerit; nun-quam tamen, vel digito extremo attigit, illa sua ini-qua prœiudicia, quibus tamē ab ea tentata fuit, Con-sessio fidei, illustrissimæ memoriæ, FRIDERICI 3. Pij, Comitis Palatini ad Rhenū, Sacri Romani Imperij Principis Electoris & Archidapiferi, Bauariæ Ducis, &c. quam heroico Spiritu, sincerè & constanter pro-fitetur, Illustrissimus & fortissimus noster Princeps, DN. IOHANNES CASIMIRVS, Comes Palatinus, &c. optimi parentis vestigiis insistens, pro cuius etiam Confessionis defensione haec disputatio Dei auspiciis, Principis autem mandatu, est instituta & iam habita. Nemo, vel conscelleratissimi Arianismi, qui à nullis Magistratibus maiore Zelo, quàm àno-stris, vindicatus; à nullarum aliarum Ecclesiarum doctoribus, maiore demonstratione Spiritus, confutatus est, absit dicto arrogantia, quàm à nostrarum Pastoribus & Doctoribus; vel impurissimi Nestorianismi, vel dicis causa nobis aspergendi, uno verbulo inter disputandum unquam commemi-nit. Manifestum enim est, non magis vere & speciose, illa opinionum haereticarum portenta, nostrae Orthodoxae Confessioni obijci posse, quàm olim Euangelio & eius fidelibus promis & Condis, Euangelistis, Apostolis caeterisque noui Testamenti Ministris, doctrinae legis, Mosis & Prophetarum abrogatio & contemtus fuit obiectus.
units.tr: IIII. Moreover, it was a great argument for our most holy cause that, although the opposing party, while we were present, never before instituted a disputation that gave us the opportunity to bring forward our arguments, which nonetheless their profession of faith dictated and demanded, but met us eight times and pursued its own cause with all its strength, it never once touched, even with the tip of a finger, those unjust prejudices of its own by which it was nonetheless tested: the Confession of Faith of the most illustrious memory of FREDERICK III the Pious, Count Palatine on the Rhine, Prince Elector of the Holy Roman Empire and Arch-Steward, Duke of Bavaria, etc., which our most illustrious and most valiant Prince, Lord JOHN CASIMIR, Count Palatine, etc., treading in the footsteps of his excellent father, professes sincerely and constantly with heroic spirit, and in defence of which this disputation was instituted and has now been held, under God's auspices and by the Prince's command. No one, not even of the most wicked Arianism, which was defended by no magistrates with greater zeal than ours and was refuted by the teachers of no other churches with greater demonstration of spirit, (let it be said without arrogance) than by the ministers and teachers of ours; nor of the most impure Nestorianism, or even to sprinkle us for show, has ever mentioned a single word during the disputation. For it is clear that those monstrous heretical opinions can be objected to our orthodox Confession no more truly and plausibly than once the abrogation and contempt of the doctrine of the law, of Moses and the Prophets, was objected to the Gospel and its faithful, to the Evangelists, Apostles and the other ministers of the New Testament.

units.la: V. Convitia autem, contentiosas voces & alia carnis opera, pessimae causae signa Pathognomonica, quoties audivi, toties mihi in mentem venit illud Ciceronis dictum: Qui in alium dicere paratus est, sibi ipsi innocentiae legem praescribit. Sumant sibi sane Censoriam Virgulam, qui sibi castae modestiaeque adolescentiae probe conscij, hoc etiam aetate virili consecuti sunt à Domino, ut sobrietatis, tem-perantiae, humilitatis, doctrinae sincerae, laude, conspicua sit illorum virilis aetas & senium: qui juve-niles cupiditates fugiunt, sectantur autem justi-tiam, temperantiam, fidem, charitatem, frugali-tatem. tatem, cum omnibus iis qui inuocant nomen Domini nostri Iesu Christi. Non autem ij, citra populi Dei suffragia, Censoriam in alios auctoritatem sibi sumant, qui Curios simulant & Bachanalia viuunt. Me equidem conuiciis anilibus, non magis quàm anserinis sibilis affici sentio, qui etiam hoc in schola Domini mei IESV CHRISTI mihi videor didicisse, ne quidem vipereos sibilos & morsus, mihi ex-ti'mescendos. Perplacet enim mihi illud Tertullia-ni: Si apud Deum deposueris iniuriam, ipse vltor est: si damnum, ipse restitutor est: si dolorem, ipse medicus est: si mortem, ipse resuscitator est.
units.tr: V. Insults, contentious voices and other works of the flesh, the pathognomonic signs of a worst cause, whenever I have heard them, have always brought to my mind that saying of Cicero: "Whoever is ready to speak against another prescribes for himself the law of innocence." Let those certainly take up the censor's rod who, well aware of their own chaste modesty and youthful purity, have also attained by the Lord in manly age that their manhood and old age be conspicuous for the praise of sobriety, temperance, humility and sincere teaching; who flee youthful desires but pursue justice, temperance, faith, charity, peacefulness, together with all those who call upon the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. But let not those, without the votes of the people of God, take to themselves authority to censure others, who pretend to be Curios and live Bacchanalian lives. For my part I feel I am no more moved by old wives' insults than by the hissing of geese; and I seem to have learned this also in the school of my Lord Jesus Christ, that not even the viperous hisses and bites are to be dreaded by me. For that saying of Tertullian pleases me greatly: "If you have deposited an injury with God, He is its avenger; if loss, He is its restorer; if pain, He is its physician; if death, He is its raiser."

units.la: Parum in schola Christi profecit, qui si audi-diat, id sibi ab homine temperantiae & humilitatis theologicae laude non admodum celebri, vitio dari, quòd posterioribus curis, quae meliores esse con-sueuerunt, locum dedit, id moleste fert: aut qui graue esse putat tacere ad vana conuicia; qui denique inimicos non diligere potest, vt maxime errores eorum, prudenter & merito auersetur, morum inci-vilitatem, improbet.
units.tr: He has made little progress in the school of Christ who, if he hears that he is faulted, by a man not very renowned for the praise of temperance and theological humility, for giving place to later cares, which are wont to be better, takes this badly; or who thinks it burdensome to be silent in the face of empty insults; who, in short, cannot love his enemies, so that he may, prudently and rightly, turn away from their errors in the greatest degree, and may disapprove of their incivility of manners.

units.la: VIdetis, Clarissimi auditores. Dei aeterni propi-tia prouidentia id nos obtinuisse, quod nobis in hac tota disputatione maxime cordi fuit, vt videlicet veritas piae nostrae confessionis de Coena Domini magis magisque confirmaretur & illustrior redderetur. Intelligitis etiam, tum quid [illegible, ~9 letters] &, eius rei causa a nobis praestitum sit, quid etiam altera pars, cui certè ex animo bene volumus, ad eam iuuandam contulerit.
units.tr: You see, most distinguished hearers, that by the favourable providence of the eternal God we have obtained what was most at heart with us in this whole disputation, namely that the truth of our pious confession concerning the Lord's Supper might be more and more confirmed and rendered more illustrious. You also understand both what [illegible, ~9 letters] and for what cause this was undertaken by us, and what the other party, to whom we certainly wish well from our hearts, has contributed toward helping it.

units.la: Prudentiae vestrae pietatisq; iam erit, animi oculis ad Deum conuersis, eius miranda & iusta iudicia adorare; & carnis ac sanguinis praeiudicijs anteferre id, quod Deum iam egisse, res ipsa loquitur.
units.tr: It will now be a matter for your prudence and piety, with the eyes of your minds turned to God, to adore His wonderful and just judgments, and to prefer to the prejudices of flesh and blood what the thing itself declares God has already done.

units.la: AD te nunc, Iuuentus studiosa, gaudium, & corona mea, me conuerto, ea perDei gratiam breuiter dicturus, quę viribus tuis seruire poterunt. Tum demum autem plerosq; iuniores in hoc coetu fide habituros orationi meae, auguror, vbi velut manu Iesu Christi prehensis, & in Theatrum eruditorum hominum producti s, de rebus magnis, (ita vt mihi totiesiam faciendū fuit, in hac splendidissima, illustrissimi Principis, illustrium, nobilissimorum hominum, corona) ex tempore aliquando respondendū erit, in Scholis Iurisconsultorum, Medicorum, Philosophorum, aut Theologorū. Scio enim quid aetas, exercitium, ardua quaestio, eruditorum conspectus, infirmitatis propriae conscientia, tandem, homini non nihil rebus aduersis & ingenti labore domito, in eiusmodi Theatro suggerant. Ac, vt de me dicam, quod res est, in tot conflictibus, & tot telis in me vnum contortis, sensi tandem animum meum obtundi, & me varietate non nihil distrahi, nulla autem re alia, quàm intemperie & importunitate, & sanctissimorū quorundā Christi seruorum, qui iam in Coelo cum eodem viuunt, satyrica insectatione, perturbatum esse (vt nihil iam de vitrea huius terreni domicilij mei valetudine, dicam) fateor ingenuè.
units.tr: To you now, studious youth, my joy and my crown, I turn, intending to say briefly, by the grace of God, the things that your strength will be able to bear. I expect that most of the younger people in this gathering will then at last place trust in my speech, when, as if led by the hand of Jesus Christ and brought onto the stage of learned men, you will sometimes have to answer extempore on great matters, in the schools of the lawyers, physicians, philosophers or theologians (as I too have had to do so many times in this most splendid assembly of the illustrious Prince and of illustrious and most noble men). For I know what age, practice, a difficult question, the sight of learned men, consciousness of one's own weakness, and finally a person who has been tamed by adversity and great labour, suggest in such a theatre. And, to speak of myself as the matter stands: among so many conflicts and so many weapons hurled together against me, I have at last felt my mind worn down and somewhat pulled apart by its distractions, and I frankly confess that it has been thrown into confusion by nothing else than the intemperance and importunity, and the satirical attacks, of certain most holy servants of Christ, who now live in heaven with him (not to mention the fragility of the health of this earthly dwelling of mine).

units.la: Sed ad rem.
units.tr: But to the matter.

units.la: I. Duae sunt ingeniorum quorundam quasique dam pestes, δοξομανία, hoc est, opinionis semel conceptae ceptæ amor inconsultus & insanus; & προσωπολημψία[?] seu nimius personæ respectus, & veluti fatuus quidam stupor, & admiratio nimia & planè inconsulta. Illa facit, ut opinio sine omni dijudicatione semel apprehensa, scientiæ loco habeatur ac vim faciat ve-ritati: Hæc efficit, ut unius adamati Magistri autori-tas, omnium rationum instar sit, & ut præcludatur intelligentiæ ianua. His malis medentur, amor veri, & studium ac admiratio unici doctoris Iesu Christi, in cuius solius verba omnes iurauimus.
units.tr: I. There are two plagues, as it were, of certain minds: δοξομανία, that is, the rash and insane love of an opinion once conceived; and προσωπολημψία [?], or excessive regard for a person, and a kind of foolish stupor and excessive, quite unconsidered admiration. The first causes an opinion, once grasped without any judgement, to be held as knowledge and to do violence to the truth; the second brings it about that the authority of one beloved master becomes the equivalent of all reasons, and the door of understanding is shut. These evils are remedied by the love of truth, and by zeal for and admiration of the one teacher, Jesus Christ, in whose words alone we have all sworn.

units.la: Quòd ergò de vita rectè instituenda præclarè dixit Seneca, id ad veritatis inquisitionem & expositionem rectè referemus. Istud, inquit Seneca, maxi-mè nobis est præstandum, ne pecorum ritu antece-dentem gregem sequamur, pergentes non quà eundum est, sed quà itur. Ne igitur unquam errantium multitudinem sequamur, si quidem saluti nostræ consultum esse volumus; sed iis nos adiungamus, qui in veritatis via sese continent, & citra turbulen-tos affectus, eandem profitentur, ac re ipsa testantur, sibi cordi esse illud Syracidis: Usque ad mortem de-certa[?] pro veritate & Dominus DEVS tuus pugnabit pro te. Ne etiam nobis persuadeamus, nunquam nos vel errasse, vel etiam errare potuisse. Stat enim il-lud Tertulliani: Aberrare nunquam, magis diuinum, quàm humanum.
units.tr: Therefore, what Seneca said well about the right ordering of life, we shall apply rightly to the search for and exposition of truth. "This," says Seneca, "above all must be ensured by us: that, in the manner of cattle, we do not follow the flock going before, proceeding not where we ought to go but where others go." Let us therefore never follow the multitude of those who err, if indeed we wish our salvation to be looked after; but let us join ourselves to those who keep to the way of truth, and, free from turbulent passions, profess the same thing and show by their deeds that the saying of the son of Sirach is dear to them: "Fight unto death for the truth, and the Lord your God will fight for you." Nor let us persuade ourselves that we have never erred, or even that we could not err. For the saying of Tertullian stands: "To err never is more divine than human."

units.la: II. Intueatur Iuventus etiam Ethnicorum quorundam Exempla, quæ virtutis causa celebrari decent, & discat studere tum paci tum publico bono, cui communes nostri hostes insidias struunt. Inter Antisthenē & Aeschinem olim simultas exorta fuit, de qua cum illi quidam illiteratus Iron dixisset; vbi iam est Philosophica vestra amicitia de qua tantopere gloriamini? Dormit, respondit Antisthenes. Ego vero paulo post illam expergefaciam. Nec diu cunctatus Aeschinem adit, &, Quando tandem, ait, desinemus nugari, ac Cerdonibus, Salsamentarijs, fullonibus, alutarijs alijsque id genus, egregijs scilicet proceribus, nos exagitandi ansam praebere? Respondit Aeschines, quum tibi quoque videbitur. Tum Antisthenes, cogita ergo, inquit, me, quum natu maior essem, pacis impetrandae causa, priorem te adijsse. Respondit alter. Profectò, vir es me multò melior, nam à me quidem offensae, abs te autem conciliatae sartaeque gratiae, initium fuit. Redierunt itaque hi duo in gratiam. Si propter communem Philosophiae professionem, & ne imperitae multitudini, obtrectandi materiam ansamque praeberent, Ethnicis illis visum est simultate deposita, amicitiae studere: quid hominibus Christianis, quibus Deus praecepit: Diligite veritatē & pacem, faciendū iudicabimus? Porrò, quoties de communi hoste Antichristo, & de eius astutia & potentia cogitamus, cur non commiseratione erga eos, qui nobis in parte aliqua doctrinae non satisfaciunt, moti, vel illud cogitamus, quod Agesilao Regi Spartano, principi Ethnico de patriae salute & gloria cogitanti, in mentem venit, quando ingenti Corinthiorum strage edita, fugientes in urbem, obsidere coepit, & coesorum cadaueribus conspectis, Eheu, ait, fatum Graeciae, quae tot fortissimos viros amisit, quorum opera vel Persarum Imperium debellare poterat? Utinam & ipsi, & ij qui nobis pacem & offerentibus & flagitantibus, de re Sacramen-taria bellum indicunt & faciunt, saltem ea re, quòd nunquam quicquam hactenus obtinere potuerunt; quod Antichristo rem gratissimam, sese à conseruis seiungèdo, faciunt, moti, socia nobiscum arma iun-gintaduersus[?] Antichristum? Utinam nobiscum in eadem acie stare, quàm seditionem inter fidei do-meticos[?], & cōmilitones (nihilo certè donis Spiritus sancti & armorum spiritualium apparatu, & alacri-tate pro defensione Euangelij, per Christi gratiam, inferiores) mouere malint; Utinam Christum in suis membris, magnificere & amare discant. Nos sane, optimi nobis conscij, tum quia veritas à nostris stat partibus, tum quia Ecclesiae causa saepe pacem illis obtulimus: non dubitamus Deum sanctae nostrae causae semper esse benedicturum.
units.tr: II. Let the youth also look at the examples of certain heathen men, which are fitting to be celebrated for the sake of virtue, and let them learn to strive for peace and for the public good, against which our common enemies lay their snares. Once a quarrel arose between Antisthenes and Aeschines, and when a certain uneducated fellow said to them, "Where now is your philosophical friendship, of which you boast so much?", Antisthenes replied: "It sleeps. But I will wake it a little later." Not long hesitating, he went to Aeschines and said: "When at last shall we stop trifling and giving to cobblers, salters, fullers, tanners and other men of that sort, who are of course outstanding nobles, an occasion to vex us?" Aeschines answered: "When it seems good to you too." Then Antisthenes said: "Consider, then, that I, being the elder, have come to you first for the sake of obtaining peace." The other replied: "Truly you are a man far better than I; for the offence came from me, but the reconciliation and the restoration of goodwill from you." And so these two were reconciled. If, for the sake of their common profession of philosophy, and so as not to give the unlearned multitude matter and occasion for detraction, those heathen men judged it right to lay aside their quarrel and pursue friendship, what shall we Christians, to whom God has commanded "Love truth and peace," judge to be our duty? Moreover, whenever we think of our common enemy, Antichrist, and of his cunning and power, why do we not, moved by compassion towards those who do not satisfy us in some part of doctrine, think also of what came into the mind of Agesilaus, the Spartan king, a heathen prince, when he was thinking of his country's safety and glory? When a great slaughter of the Corinthians had been made and they were fleeing into the city, and he began to besiege it, and seeing the corpses of those cut down, he said: "Alas, the fate of Greece, which has lost so many most brave men, by whose labour it might have been able to subdue the empire of the Persians!"
